principle: Set the game's risk by its target player, not by your own skill
why: Sakurai wanted the first Kirby to be as accessible as possible for new players, so inhaling and flying both lowered the risks they faced, even when staff asked 'Are you sure about this?'. In his view more game essence means less broad appeal, and a minor risk to a veteran can be a brick wall to a newcomer. The same reasoning ran the other way when the audience changed: Brawl slowed down for casual Wii players, and Uprising aimed at hardcore players.
how_to_apply: Write down the target player before tuning any risk. For newcomers, soften the harshest penalties while keeping some (flight over pits, but falling still costs a life). For experts, let them raise the risk themselves. Re-check risk whenever the platform or audience shifts.
anti_pattern: Making a game unreasonably hard so it lasts longer; tuning risk to the development team's skill.
example: Kirby's Dream Land: inhale before an approaching enemy gets dangerous, six hits of health, flight at any time. Melee was so fast it was hard on newcomers, so Brawl's speed was a little slower. Uprising's Fiend's Cauldron let players bet hearts on higher intensity, though Sakurai later felt the game came out too hardcore.
review_question: Who is this game for, and does its harshest penalty suit that player?
keywords: target audience difficulty risk accessibility beginners casual hardcore penalty kirby dream land brawl

principle: Layer optional depth on a core that a novice can finish
why: When Kirby's Adventure came out, the NES market had matured and few beginners were starting on it, so the game had to satisfy both groups. The copy ability sat on top of inhale-and-spit: novices could finish with the core, while experienced players dug into abilities for tricks. Extras for one audience were kept off the critical path. Smash's configurable rules carried the same idea into multiplayer: play what you want, how you want.
how_to_apply: Play through using only the core verbs and confirm the game can be finished that way. Put depth systems and audience-specific extras where players choose them: a map entrance, a rule toggle, an optional mode. Make sure the depth layer gives each encounter something to look forward to.
anti_pattern: Requiring the depth system to progress; forcing extras on players who don't want them.
example: Kirby's Adventure: copy abilities, plus three one-button minigames entered from the world map. Super Smash Bros.: chaotic four-player matches with items, or tense one-on-one without. The first Kirby was made for beginners but has enough 'oomph' that advanced players enjoy the controls.
review_question: Can a novice finish using only the core, and what does the optional layer give veterans?
keywords: optional depth layered design beginners and experts copy ability optional content accessibility skill ceiling kirby's adventure

principle: Build the concept as the answer to a named problem
why: Sakurai says most of his concepts are logical: they solve a problem. He felt combo-heavy fighters lost push and pull, since after the first hit the opponent's skill stopped mattering, so Smash used accumulated damage and ring-outs. Too many games took too long to beat, so Kirby Super Star became an omnibus. He felt FPS and TPS games were stuck in by-the-book theory, so Uprising rethought the genre. For Meteos he first worked out the genre's risk and reward, then asked whether blocks even had to be erased.
how_to_apply: Write the pain point of the genre or the brief in one sentence, then design a core rule that removes it. Test the answer: does it change what the player actually does, or only what the action is called? If it only renames, keep going.
anti_pattern: Cosmetic novelty that renames the standard verb; treating an 'antithesis' as rejection rather than a response to something you respect.
example: Smash's accumulated damage and ring-outs; Meteos' matched blocks that blast off into space, enabling secondary ignitions and air docking; Kirby Super Star's cork board of short scenarios.
review_question: What specific problem does our core rule solve, and does it change what the player does?
keywords: concept problem solving genre innovation push and pull core rule smash bros meteos originality

principle: Let the platform's unique strength and the market gap shape the concept
why: For Kid Icarus: Uprising, glasses-free 3D meant depth had to be part of the fun, and Touch! Generations already covered casual DS players, so he made a meaty shooter for hardcore players. For Smash for 3DS and Wii U he framed the platforms as the 'one' and the 'many' and gave each version modes built on that. The N64 analog stick inspired flick input, GameCube streaming audio allowed orchestral music in Melee, and the Wii's built-in online made online play essential for Brawl. He also warns against shoehorning in every function of new hardware.
how_to_apply: List what the target hardware does that others can't and which audiences competitors already serve, then aim the concept at the gap. If shipping on several platforms, give each at least one mode built on its own strength while sharing mechanics, animation and balance. Skip peripheral functions that don't serve the game.
anti_pattern: Versions that differ only in graphical power; using every gimmick a device offers.
example: Smash Run on 3DS (five minutes of power-up collecting on a huge map, since everyone has their own screen) versus 8-Player Smash and Smash Tour on Wii U. Brawl deliberately didn't use every Nunchuk or pointer function.
review_question: What does our platform do uniquely, and which part of our design depends on it?
keywords: platform hardware strengths market gap concept multiplatform kid icarus uprising smash 3ds wii u flick input

principle: Choose the concept your situation can finish, and uniquely enables
why: Two prototypes won praise, but the team needed a finished game soon and the RC adventure would have taken two years, so the fighter became Smash. A racer was judged quicker to make than an action game to accompany the Kirby anime. Kirby's Adventure went to the NES because setting up an SNES environment would take too long. Ultimate kept the same studio, team and tools on similar hardware, which made bringing back every fighter feasible: Sakurai saw it as the one chance.
how_to_apply: Estimate each candidate concept's development time. Inventory what carries over (team, tools, assets, hardware architecture) and look for the bold idea that inventory makes cheap. Pick the concept that fits both the schedule and that one-time opportunity.
anti_pattern: Chasing a concept the team can't finish in time; ignoring an ambition that only your current situation makes affordable.
example: Dragon King: The Fighting Game chosen over the RC robot adventure; Kirby Air Ride as the quicker-to-make companion to the anime; Ultimate's 'Everyone is here!', with only seven missing veterans to rebuild.
review_question: Given our team, tools and remaining time, which concept can we actually finish, and what does our situation make uniquely possible?
keywords: feasibility scope concept selection production continuity schedule smash prototype ultimate everyone is here

principle: Change a feature's context before cutting it
why: On the NES's larger screen Kirby could fly past almost any challenge. Sakurai considered removing flight but changed its context instead: a bigger info panel limited vertical space and made characters read bigger, mid-boss fights stayed on one screen, and flight got slower, and he felt it ended up nicely balanced. Kirby Super Star made co-op scrolling work by restructuring roles (a lead the camera follows and a Helper who can be off-camera) instead of dropping the request.
how_to_apply: When a signature mechanic breaks balance or a request seems impossible, list the context levers (screen space, arena bounds, speed, camera, player roles, HUD) and try them before cutting the feature.
anti_pattern: Cutting a signature mechanic that a context change could rebalance; giving every co-op player equal pull on the camera in a jump-heavy side-scroller.
example: Kirby's Adventure's flight; Kirby Super Star's Helper system with its 'Space Jump' warp back to the lead. In Dream Land he accepted that flight could skip enemies because the Game Boy screen was so small.
review_question: Before cutting this feature, which context lever have we tried changing?
keywords: rebalance context camera co-op helper flight hud signature mechanic kirby's adventure kirby super star

principle: Build variety as rule-changing parameters on one shared core
why: Kirby Air Ride's machines feel totally different but share one underlying behavior: apart from star versus bike types, everything is parameters, so a machine's character changes by tweaking a few numbers. Each Meteos planet changes block shapes, field width, launch behavior, music and sound, so the controls feel drastically different and players pick favorites. Smash for 3DS/Wii U's 'variable character strength' framework powered several modes at once. Uprising's weapons change Pit's speed, not just damage.
how_to_apply: Implement one shared behavior, then express each vehicle, stage, character or weapon as a parameter set that changes how it plays (size, gravity, speed, field shape, piece types) plus its own audio. Keep strength-varying layers out of modes that need a level playing field.
anti_pattern: Character select that only swaps art or barely changes skills; separate code for every variant.
example: Air Ride's machines; Meteos planets such as Boggob (gains height with each jump), Hevendor (blocks vanish when matched) and Brabbit (moves very slowly); Smash Run, Smash Tour, custom moves, Mii Fighters and amiibo on one parameter layer.
review_question: Do our characters, stages or vehicles change the rules, or only the art?
keywords: parameters variety data-driven characters stages vehicles shared behavior kirby air ride meteos planets variable strength

principle: Tune and test on the final build and the real hardware
why: Meteos' game speed was tied to processing speed, so a late optimization made it faster and harder than Sakurai's per-planet tuning intended. Sodatete! Kouchuu Ouja Mushiking was tuned on a custom board and never played on the production handheld, and the Mushi gets hungry faster than planned. Smash Ultimate's CPU fighters felt too hard at launch for reasons he still doesn't know. 'When you're working with computers, sometimes there's no telling what you might get.'
how_to_apply: Lock processing speed and frame timing before final balance tuning. After any optimization, replay difficulty and timer-driven systems on the retail unit. When a launch problem is too risky to fix at its core, ship a narrow, contained fix.
anti_pattern: Shipping without playing on production hardware; changing processing speed after tuning.
example: Ultimate's fix lowered Challenger fight difficulty and added a Very Easy setting to World of Light instead of touching core CPU functions, which would have meant re-testing much of the game.
review_question: Has the final balance been checked on production hardware after the last optimization?
keywords: final hardware testing tuning processing speed timing bugs patch retail unit meteos mushiking ultimate cpu

principle: Give each sequel one headline concept its new situation makes possible
why: Each Smash sequel had a clear headline tied to what had changed. Melee: power up Smash by leaps and bounds on far stronger hardware. Brawl: online support and a single-player mode of appropriate length for the Wii. Smash for 3DS/Wii U: the one and the many. Ultimate: 'Everyone is here!'. A sequel that repeats the original at the same scale can expect roughly half the sales.
how_to_apply: Name the sequel's headline in one line and tie it to what is new (hardware, audience, team continuity). Then list every element of the game (characters, stages, graphics, effects, animation, sound, play feel, extras) and set an upgrade target for each.
anti_pattern: A generic 'more of the same'; same scale and similar content.
example: Melee upgraded fighters, stages, graphics, effects, animation, sound, content, play feel, items and bonus features, and used streaming for orchestral music. Without Sakurai, Brawl might have been Melee's 26 fighters plus online.
review_question: What is this sequel's one-line headline, and does every element have an upgrade target?
keywords: sequel headline concept upgrade melee brawl ultimate series franchise iteration

principle: Treat hard limits as design fuel
why: Kirby's Dream Land was largely designed for 512 kilobits, so art was shared and flipped and Whispy Woods was one mirrored piece. With scarce processing, enemy paths were hand-placed with no terrain collision, which also left room for lively, bouncy animation. Uprising made standard enemies four or five times Pit's size for a small handheld screen. The 3DS's LCD led to slower knockback so action stayed readable.
how_to_apply: When memory, processing or screen size is scarce, write down the limit and ask which design answers it (reused and mirrored art, authored patterns instead of simulation, bigger targets, slower motion) before cutting content.
anti_pattern: Treating limits only as subtraction; detail spent where nobody looks.
example: Waddle Dee and Waddle Doo share a back half, 'two characters using the ROM space of only 1.5'. Big bosses in Dream Land meant slightly off-target attacks still hit. Ultimate's music was compressed to fit a roughly 16 GB cartridge.
review_question: Which of our limits could become a design idea instead of a cut?
keywords: constraints hardware limits rom memory budget small screen design under constraints kirby dream land

principle: When a mode is out of budget, rebuild it from strengths you already have
why: At Ultimate's scale a Subspace Emissary-style mode and Trophies were too costly, and a string of versus fights would satisfy nobody. Spirits reused Smash's borrowed characters, worlds and sounds to recreate situations from their source games, and World of Light tied those battles into one story. Smash Run took City Trial's rules. Melee's Trophies brought in characters who couldn't be playable.
how_to_apply: Inventory the assets and systems you already have and design the missing mode around them. Pick lightweight formats when you want volume. Let players over-power themselves as a chosen difficulty, but give fewer rewards when they do.
anti_pattern: Solo content that is one versus battle after another; expensive bespoke formats where a cheap one would scale.
example: Spirits are earned by winning battles that recreate their source games, can be leveled, and pay out less when the player is overpowered.
review_question: What existing assets could carry the mode we can't afford to build from scratch?
keywords: budget reuse assets solo mode spirits world of light single-player content scale collectibles

principle: Earn replay value with varied, fun play, not punishing difficulty
why: NES games were often made hard so they wouldn't be beaten too quickly, which left beginners out in the cold; Sakurai's answer was that a fun game gets played again and again. Kirby Air Ride rejected a design where everyone converges on one perfect line and broadened the possible play types instead, most of all in City Trial. Randomness makes repeated play go differently.
how_to_apply: Add at least one mode built for variety rather than perfection (a sandbox, random power-ups and events) so players don't converge on one method. Make failure cheap and the next attempt worth seeing.
anti_pattern: Difficulty as a substitute for content; designing only around time-shaving perfection.
example: Kirby's Dream Land is short (about 20 minutes for experienced players) yet sold over 5 million copies. City Trial's power-ups and stadiums make every session different.
review_question: Why would someone play this again tomorrow, other than it being hard?
keywords: replayability replay value variety sandbox randomness difficulty longevity city trial kirby dream land

principle: When adapting, keep the proven core and spend effort on the new format
why: The arcade Mushiking already had push and pull (rock-paper-scissors with each Mushi specializing in one shape), so Sakurai didn't have to think hard about it and spent his effort on the pet format: smoothing growth-stage walls, a Mushi that grazes instead of scarfing food, hidden behaviors. In licensed work fans want faithfulness first, so invent where the source shows little: Fox and Captain Falcon are pilots who do little else in their games, which gave room for the Falcon Punch.
how_to_apply: Identify the proven loop of the source and keep it. Put design effort into what the new format adds. Stay faithful where fans care, invent where the source is silent, and redesign characters to fit their new role.
anti_pattern: Rewriting what fans love; reinventing a core that already works.
example: Mushiking's grazing Mushi and its schedule that shifts when you wake it early; Meta Knight's mask slit reshaped for each game's role and era.
review_question: What does the source already do well that we should keep, and where is it silent so we can invent?
keywords: adaptation licensed games source material faithfulness port spin-off mushiking falcon punch

principle: When delegated core work stalls, step in with fresh specs
why: After a year of delegated development on Kirby Air Ride, not one Warp Star worked properly. At the lead programmer's request Sakurai returned as director, they hashed out new specs and rebuilt the game logic, and it was finished in three and a half months, helped by courses and machines that were mostly done. Iwata likewise worked with Melee's programmers to find code bugs in its final stretch.
how_to_apply: Set a checkpoint for the core gameplay. If it still doesn't work, have the person with the vision rewrite the specs and rebuild the logic on the existing assets, briefing every discipline together so instructions aren't distorted in relay.
anti_pattern: Leaving core gameplay delegated while it stalls for months.
example: Kirby Air Ride's rebuild; on Uprising, instructions relayed through a planner sometimes came back as the opposite of what he wanted, so from Smash for 3DS/Wii U on he briefed everyone at once.
review_question: Is the core gameplay actually working at this checkpoint, and who will step in if not?
keywords: delegation rebuild specs director intervention stalled development kirby air ride melee recovery

principle: If people don't get the concept, explain its depth yourself
why: Right before the original Smash shipped, sales staff, wholesalers and magazines rejected the idea of Nintendo characters fighting and called it shallow. Sakurai's push-and-pull documentation was ignored, so he turned it into the Smash Bros. DOJO!! players' guide site, writing the HTML himself. Brawl's Dojo later posted a new detail every weekday in six languages.
how_to_apply: Write a plain explanation of how to play and why the game is deep, in the words of the person who knows it best, and publish it on a regular schedule where players will find it.
anti_pattern: Assuming a new kind of game will explain itself or that the press will do it for you.
example: Smash Bros. DOJO!! for the original game; daily updates during Brawl's development.
review_question: If someone thinks our game is shallow, where can they read why it isn't?
keywords: marketing explanation players guide dojo new concept communication smash bros

principle: Check a new technique fits the team and the game before adopting it
why: Mid-development, Kirby Super Star switched to CG backgrounds following games like Donkey Kong Country. Sakurai doesn't think it turned out especially well: the staff weren't familiar with it and it didn't suit Kirby's pieced-together terrain. Still, he says, learning new skills matters because what you make today leads to what you make tomorrow.
how_to_apply: Before switching to a trendy technique mid-project, confirm the team knows it and that it suits how your levels are built. If you go ahead anyway, treat it as skill-building and budget for the learning.
anti_pattern: Following an art trend that doesn't fit how the game is built.
example: Kirby Super Star's pre-rendered CG backgrounds.
review_question: Does the team know this technique, and does it fit how our content is built?
keywords: art direction technique adoption trend pipeline change mid-project kirby super star cg backgrounds

principle: For a fixed-scope side project, script it all and pilot it first
why: Running a channel next to a large game was only feasible if all the content was decided in advance, so Sakurai wrote every script before recording, with a fixed episode count per category. A pilot of three real episodes tested whether he could really do it and won Nintendo's cooperation. He favored speed over perfection and cleared every review the day it arrived.
how_to_apply: When the content can be known up front, plan and write all of it before production, pilot a few pieces at final quality, and track everything in one spreadsheet that holds the release order and progress.
anti_pattern: Improvising long-form content while juggling another big job.
example: Masahiro Sakurai on Creating Games: a few hundred one-line topics, 256 planned episodes, and a pilot of C03, C11 and D03.
review_question: Is the scope fixed enough to plan completely, and has a pilot proved we can deliver it?
keywords: side project content planning pilot scripting channel production schedule masahiro sakurai on creating games
